clue.text: Help backward people and get a mouthful

indicators.note: backward tells us to read the word for help from right to left

parts.note: to help is to aid
a tribe is a people or clan

explanation.surface: An instruction to aid a retreating crowd, which earns you a scolding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a mouthful' here is a telling-off, and the indicator 'backward' turns only the word for help.
explanation.definitionFit: Informally, giving someone a mouthful means a long angry tirade, which is a bitter verbal attack.

clue.text: One sleeps around

parts.note: reads as a promiscuous person, but means someone who sleeps rough wherever they can, in doorways and hostels

explanation.surface: A remark about somebody with a busy love life.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang a dosser is a homeless person who beds down wherever they can, so 'around' means here and there, not with many partners.
explanation.definitionFit: A British slang term for a vagrant who kips rough in various places around town.

clue.text: Turkish official tea bag masher

indicators.note: a masher crushes and rearranges, so the letters of the following words get mixed up

explanation.surface: A Turkish dignitary who squashes his tea bag against the cup.
explanation.walkthrough: 'masher' signals the anagram of TEA BAG.
explanation.definitionFit: An atabeg was a hereditary governor or regent title in the Seljuk Turkish states.

clue.text: Junk consumed has to go round

parts.note: rot is nonsense, rubbish, junk
consumed means ate

explanation.surface: Rubbish that has been eaten must be passed round.
explanation.definitionFit: To rotate is to turn or spin about a centre, that is to revolve.

clue.text: Early example of an oxymoron?

definitions.meaning: ahead of schedule, sooner than expected
the phrase read literally puts something ahead of time itself, a self-contradiction

explanation.surface: A suggestion that one kind of contradiction comes ahead of the others.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the whimsical second reading: nothing can come ahead of time, so the phrase contradicts itself.
explanation.definitionFit: An old-fashioned adverb for prematurely, ahead of the proper moment.

clue.text: She takes a short step

indicators.note: short means the word for step loses its final letter

parts.note: a stride is a long step

explanation.surface: A woman taking a little pace forward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short' trims STRIDE to STRID; A comes from the clue as written.
explanation.definitionFit: Astrid is a woman's given name, so a female, referred to as she.

clue.text: Where there's very little point to motor to London?

parts.note: S, south, is a compass point
a motor is a car
the City is London's financial district, the City of London

explanation.surface: A question about driving into London to find hardly anyone there.
explanation.walkthrough: Both 'to' words are links; the City is the old square mile at London's heart.
explanation.definitionFit: Scarcity is a state of shortage, a situation in which a thing is in short supply.

clue.text: Sort of treatment soldiers face

parts.note: REME is the Royal Electrical and Mechanical Engineers, a British army corps
a dial is the face of a clock or watch; also slang for a person's face

explanation.surface: Some kind of rough handling that army men must endure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'treatment' and 'face' suggest soldiers confronting hardship, but REME is a corps of the British army and DIAL is slang for a face.
explanation.definitionFit: Remedial describes corrective treatment intended to put something right.

clue.text: What might be said surrounded by rows and sneers

indicators.note: surrounded by tells us the scrambled word sits inside the word for rows

parts.note: dins are noisy rows, rackets

indicators.note: what might be suggests the word that follows could become something else, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Words spoken amid rows of people, met with scorn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What might be' is an unusual anagram signal and 'surrounded by' the container; rows here are noises, not lines of seats.
explanation.definitionFit: Disdains as a verb means scorns or looks down on, the attitude behind a sneer.

clue.text: Begin with leading upper class character

parts.note: the leading actor or performer is the star
a toff is British slang for an upper-class person

explanation.surface: Setting out in the company of a posh lead player.
explanation.walkthrough: TOFF is British slang for a posh person.
explanation.definitionFit: To start off is a phrasal verb meaning to commence or set out.

clue.text: Rally driver taken short on Greek island

indicators.note: taken short means the driver's name loses its last letter

parts.note: Pat Moss was a famous British rally driver, sister of Stirling Moss

explanation.surface: A motorsport competitor caught needing the loo while on holiday in Greece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taken short' is British for urgently needing a toilet, but here it cuts the final S from PAT MOSS.
explanation.definitionFit: Patmos is a small Aegean island in the Dodecanese, where St John wrote Revelation.

clue.text: English readers make the signs of the times

definitions.text: make the signs of the times

parts.note: lectors are readers, especially of lessons in church or lecturers at a university

explanation.surface: A claim that English-speaking readers produce the symbols of the age.
explanation.walkthrough: The times sign is the multiplication cross, X, which voters mark on a ballot paper; the definition is a cryptic description of voters.
explanation.definitionFit: Voters mark an X on their ballot, and X is also the multiplication or times symbol.

clue.text: Lack of enthusiasm over the church backing opera

indicators.note: over means the reversed opera is laid across and around the church abbreviation
backing means the title of the opera is reversed

parts.note: Aida is Verdi's opera
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A grumble about apathy toward the church supporting operatic productions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing' reverses the opera only; 'over' is used as a container signal, the reversed title spread across the church.
explanation.definitionFit: Acedia is spiritual sloth or apathy, a listless indifference.

clue.text: They look down on lesser breeds as seen in mother's row

definitions.text: They look down on lesser breeds

parts.note: ma is mother, so mother's is ma's
a terrace is a row of joined houses

explanation.surface: Snobbish neighbours living on mum's street.
explanation.walkthrough: TERRACE is the British word for a row of houses built joined together.
explanation.definitionFit: The master race is the supremacist notion of a superior people who scorn others.

clue.text: Side in stress being seldom on track of late

definitions.text: being seldom on track of late

indicators.note: in places the word for side within the word for stress

parts.note: strain is stress or tension
a side is a team in sport

explanation.surface: A team under pressure, rarely in form these days.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is the container signal; the definition is a wry description of locomotives that rarely run nowadays.
explanation.definitionFit: Steam locomotives now run on railway lines only rarely, as heritage excursions.

clue.text: Prickly plant in a container shut carelessly

parts.note: a can is a container

indicators.note: carelessly suggests the word is jumbled rather than properly arranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A thorny plant inside a tin whose lid was closed sloppily.
explanation.walkthrough: 'carelessly' rearranges SHUT into THUS.
explanation.definitionFit: Acanthus is a genus of spiny-leaved plants, also called bear's breeches.

clue.text: Holdall?

parts.note: a bag for carrying things, but read as the thing that holds all that exists

explanation.surface: A travel bag.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark asks you to read holdall as 'holds all'.
explanation.definitionFit: The cosmos contains all that exists, so it literally holds everything.

clue.text: Sweetheart clued in a different way

indicators.note: in a different way tells us the letters are arranged differently

explanation.surface: A lover hinted at by an unusual crossword clue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'different way' rearranges the letters of CLUED IN A; Dulcinea is Don Quixote's idealised lady.
explanation.definitionFit: Dulcinea, Don Quixote's idealised lady, became a byword for a beloved.

clue.text: Put down rug inside — perfect!

indicators.note: inside places the word for rug within the word for put down

parts.note: to put down food is to eat it, consume it
a mat is a small rug

explanation.surface: An instruction to lay the carpet indoors, followed by delight at the result.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put down' suggests laying a rug, but means eating, as in putting food away; 'inside' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Consummate as an adjective means supremely skilled or flawless.

clue.text: The archdeacon always put on outward show

parts.note: an archdeacon is styled the Venerable, abbreviated Ven
e'er is the poetic contraction of ever, always

explanation.surface: A churchman who constantly kept up appearances.
explanation.walkthrough: In the Church of England an archdeacon's title is 'the Venerable', shortened to Ven.
explanation.definitionFit: A veneer is a thin surface layer, figuratively a superficial facade.

clue.text: Street garb featured in a disco

parts.note: a robe is a garment, garb

explanation.surface: Urban clothing spotted at a nightclub.
explanation.definitionFit: A strobe light flashes rapidly and is a fixture of nightclub dance floors.

clue.text: Girl doing termly revision

indicators.note: a revision reworks the word, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A schoolgirl studying for her end-of-term exams.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revision' suggests exam study but signals the anagram of TERMLY.
explanation.definitionFit: Myrtle is a female forename, so it names a girl.

clue.text: New member has a month on the rocks

parts.note: Nov is the abbreviation for November
on the rocks means served with ice

explanation.surface: A newcomer to the club whose month has gone badly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on the rocks' suggests ruin, but a drink on the rocks is served with ICE.
explanation.definitionFit: A novice is a beginner, someone newly joined, as in a religious order.

clue.text: Clerical writer (not English)

indicators.note: not means the letter for English is left out of the writer's name

parts.note: J. B. Priestley was an English novelist and playwright

explanation.surface: A churchly author who happens not to be English.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not' removes one E from PRIESTLEY.
explanation.definitionFit: Priestly means relating to priests, hence of the clergy.

clue.text: Courtesy titles involve the Queen having considerable bills

indicators.note: involve means the titles wrap round the royal abbreviation

parts.note: Hon, short for Honourable, is a courtesy title, so Hons
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the Queen

explanation.surface: Aristocrats who bring the monarch in on some hefty invoices.
explanation.walkthrough: Bills here are beaks, not invoices: these wading birds have long ones.
explanation.definitionFit: Herons are wading birds with long, dagger-like beaks.

clue.text: 30 centimetres discalced?

definitions.meaning: a foot is 30.48 centimetres, so 30 centimetres is only just short of a foot
discalced means unshod, as in friars who go without shoes

explanation.surface: A measurement followed by a rare word for shoeless.
explanation.walkthrough: The first reading is whimsical: 30 centimetres is barely a foot, read as two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Discalced describes religious orders who go unshod, with naked soles.

clue.text: Comprehend saying of repeated alternation

parts.note: to see is to understand, comprehend
a saw is an old saying or proverb

explanation.surface: Understanding a proverb about going back and forth.
explanation.definitionFit: A seesaw movement is a continual up-and-down or back-and-forth swing.

clue.text: French back behind London hearing an old tune

indicators.note: hearing tells us the words are judged by how they sound when spoken

parts.note: what comes after London in the title of the old tune the Londonderry Air is Derry Air

explanation.surface: A Frenchman's backside following a Londoner who listens to a folk melody.
explanation.walkthrough: 'an old tune' points to the Londonderry Air; the part behind 'London' is DERRY AIR, which 'hearing' turns into the French word for behind, now English slang for the bottom.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is borrowed from French, where it means at the rear, and in English it means the buttocks.
